body:
（本文作者为 Chelsea_Sun，钛媒体经授权发布）
NextFin News — The race in AI video is less about who can render the most striking clip than about who can sustain low prices and still hold the customer relationship.
Google has cut the list price of a mainstream 720p generation tier to well under a dollar per several seconds of output, with multi-turn editing that bills each revision. Chinese vendors have followed with promotional rates measured in fractions of a yuan per second. Creators who once treated every generation as a budget decision now treat retries as routine. Capability gaps on public leaderboards have narrowed to ranges that many practitioners describe as interchangeable for ordinary shots. Model switches increasingly turn on speed, price, and workflow fit rather than a decisive quality gap.
That pattern points away from a durable product monopoly and toward a commodity generation layer sitting on costly infrastructure.
OpenAI’s Sora illustrated the strain. The product launched with unusual consumer attention, then shut within about half a year. Reporting at the time pointed to daily losses on the order of a million dollars and compute intensity far above ordinary text chat. Video generation does not scale like classic software: more users mean more inference, not thinner marginal cost. If each paid second fails to cover chips, power, and serving, growth widens the deficit.
No major pure-play video model company has publicly claimed steady profits. Even the strongest Chinese revenue stories still point to breakeven years away. Fixed costs—training runs, teams, data centers—remain large. Variable costs rise with every successful push for adoption. The central commercial question is whether a generation request is a profitable unit or a subsidized sample.
Companies that remain active are not escaping that cost structure. They are absorbing it inside broader businesses.
Google can price video aggressively because the same customer may pay through cloud contracts, workspace subscriptions, or advertising, and because in-house accelerators lower the cash cost of each inference relative to rivals that rent capacity. Video tools are spread across creator products, enterprise cloud, and ad workflows, so a cheap clip can pull spending elsewhere in the stack.
ByteDance treats generation as upstream supply for a chain it already operates: story IP, scripting aids, timeline editors, short-drama and short-video distribution, then advertising and e-commerce. AI reduces the cost of producing episodes; a large share of short-drama cash still goes into paid distribution, much of it on ByteDance surfaces. The model line can look only modestly profitable in isolation while the group captures traffic and ad budgets downstream. API sales through its cloud arm add a second channel aimed at studios and toolmakers.
Kuaishou’s Kling effort splits internal use and external brand. Inside the group, generation supports ad creatives, commerce video, and drama previsualization. Outside, a more independent commercial posture—and a large funding round after a carve-out—extends the runway to pursue professional pipelines and overseas API demand. Reported revenue has risen quickly; public commentary still places meaningful quarterly profit in a later year.
In each case, video functions as a feature of a larger commercial system. OpenAI, under tighter capital-market pressure and without a comparable short-video distribution or advertising engine, treated Sora as a line that failed a narrower test.
Lower unit prices will pull generation into advertising, short drama, product clips, and social drafts that could not justify earlier rates. They will not, by themselves, produce a healthy stand-alone model industry. When blind evaluations show near ties among several systems, buyers gain leverage. Platforms that control demand can treat model suppliers as interchangeable. Platforms that control both demand and distribution can keep cutting list prices while still showing gains in cloud revenue, ad volume, or content cost.
Technical parity and falling prices are established facts. The structural outcome is clearer still: mass demand for text inference grew inside products people already used; mass demand for video inference is concentrating where firms already own audiences and monetization. Until each generation second reliably covers its cost, advantage will favor companies that never required AI video to stand alone as a clean profit-and-loss business.
